claims.statement: In two placebo-controlled trials from one San Francisco team, in non-depressed men who have sex with men with methamphetamine dependence who all received weekly counselling (60 men treated for 12 weeks; 120 cisgender men and transgender women treated for 24 weeks and followed 12 weeks after stopping), mirtazapine lowered the modelled weekly probability of a methamphetamine-positive urine compared with placebo: relative risk 0.57 (95% CI 0.35–0.93) at 12 weeks in the first trial and 0.67 (0.51–0.87) at 12 weeks in the second, with net relative risks of 0.75 (0.56–1.00) at 24 weeks and 0.73 (0.57–0.96) 12 weeks after medication stopped. Most urine samples stayed positive in both arms (66% vs 78% of samples provided at week 12 of the second trial), end-of-treatment abstinence did not differ significantly (18% vs 8%; OR 2.50, 0.80–7.61), adherence measured by electronic pill containers was below 50% in both arms, and drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine. The two trials share investigators, site, population and analysis model, so they are not independent replications.
claims.magnitude: First trial (n=60): RR 0.57 (0.35–0.93) at 12 weeks; raw final-visit positivity 44% vs 63% (editors' RR 0.71, 0.42–1.18). Second trial (n=120): RR 0.67 (0.51–0.87) at 12 weeks; net RR 0.75 (0.56–1.00) at 24 weeks and 0.73 (0.57–0.96) at 36 weeks; raw positivity 66% vs 78%, 63% vs 74% and 71% vs 88%; end-of-treatment abstinence 18% vs 8% (OR 2.50, 0.80–7.61).
